Method/Genome assembly and variant calling

Reference-free SNP calling

Identify SNPs shared across samples directly from split k-mers, without a reference genome.

When to use this method

Use when

  • No suitable reference genome exists for your samples.
  • Samples span lineages diverse enough that a single reference would introduce mapping bias.
  • You need fast SNP distances for screening or a first look at a new collection.

Use another method when

  • A later step needs genome positions, such as recombination filtering, because only variable sites are kept. Use Reference-based SNP calling instead.
  • Indels carry signal you want to keep. Use Reference-based consensus calling instead.

Operation

Genome assembly and variant calling

Implementations

  • SKA

Needs

Clean reads

Produces

SNP-only alignment

How it works

Variation is detected from split k-mers, which are k-mers that match across samples except at their middle base. SNPs are found directly by comparing samples, so results do not depend on choosing a reference.

The output is an alignment of variable sites only. It is ready for tree building, but it carries no genome positions and does not capture indels. Because positions are unknown, recombination filtering cannot be applied afterward.

Used by protocols

Specified by

  • Bacterial phylogenomic surveillanceStep 3
  • Fungal phylogenomic surveillanceStep 3

Alternative methods

  • De novo assemblyAssemble each sample's genome from its reads alone, without a reference.
  • Reference-based SNP callingMap reads to a reference, call SNPs, and combine samples into a core SNP alignment of positions present in every sample.
  • Reference-based consensus callingMap reads to a reference and write a complete consensus sequence for each sample, including indels.
